transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-12-01 15:00 UTC | Duration: ~42 min | Recording: yes
Attendees: Samantha Lee (Redwood AE), Miguel Alvarez (Redwood SE), Priya Shah (Orion Head of ML), Liam O'Connor (Platform), Marta Rivera (Security), Ben (Product)

Summary: quick hosted API walkthrough focusing on chat/text gen basics — streaming, key params (temp, max_tokens, top_p), retries/ idempotency, and how Redwood handles latency/cost tradeoffs. Security questions on data retention and KMS; agreed to next steps: send security pack, pricing, schedule POC scoping.

[00:00] Samantha: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'll hand off to Miguel for the live demo after a 5 minute context check. Priya, can you briefly share your main use case?
[00:15] Priya: Sure, hi, thanks. We're building a insights assistant that summarizes market reports and answers analyst Qs. Throughput is about 20 qps with bursts to 80 qps during morning ingest, latency target sub-500ms for short chats, and cost is obviously a factor. Also security — SOC2 plus customer-managed keys would be ideal.
[00:40] Samantha: Perfect. That matches a lot of our other customers. For this call we'll show our Hosted API for chat/text gen — streaming responses, how to tune params to balance cost/latency/quality, and our retry/backoff behavior for transient errors.
[01:05] Miguel: Ok jumping into the console, give me a sec — loading. (audio: keyboard) Right so here is the API playground, you can do chat or text endpoints. We'll demo a chat request streaming back tokens.
[01:30] Miguel: Example payload: model: "redwood-chat-3b" (we also have 7b and 13b variants), messages: [{role: "user", content: "Summarize Q3 market trends for fintech"}], and important params: temperature (0.0-1.2), max_tokens, top_p, n, stop sequences.
[02:05] Miguel: I'm going to enable streaming — you can see partial tokens come in for lower front-end latency. Streaming is over server-sent events / chunked responses in the SDKs. It reduces perceived latency while token generation continues.
[02:30] Priya: Do you support token-level deltas or do you get whole chunks?
[02:35] Miguel: We stream token chunks/partial deltas. The SDK exposes callbacks for partial tokens and a final event with metadata. On the console we show the streaming bar and token rate.
[03:00] Liam: How do you recommend tuning temperature and top_p for summarization vs creative responses?
[03:10] Miguel: For summarization keep temperature low, 0-0.3, and top_p around 0.8-1.0; lower max_tokens helps cost. For creative generation raise temperature to 0.7+. We also suggest using stop sequences to limit hallucination for structured outputs.
[03:40] Miguel: Quick note on caching: prefix/KV cache is automatic for hosted requests when identical prefixes are common — it can shave tokens and cost. For chat with stateful histories, we support partial KV cache reuse for repeated system messages.
[04:15] Marta: From a security standpoint, where does the data live and what's your retention policy?
[04:20] Samantha: Hosted keeps data for 30 days by default for debugging, we have options to not persist or auto-purge with enterprise plans. We'll send the SOC2 and retention docs. We support customer KMS for private deployments; for hosted we offer managed KMS and bring-your-own-key for Dedicated/Private plans.
[04:55] Miguel: Back to retries — our SDK defaults to idempotent retries for non-streaming create requests; streaming is treated carefully because partial tokens can be received. We use a safe retry window and give a retry token in responses to coordinate resumes. For high reliability we recommend retry/backoff with jitter — our SDKs do that out of the box.
[05:30] Priya: So if the socket disconnects mid-stream, client can resume?
[05:35] Miguel: Yes, in many cases the SDK can resume from the last confirmed token using the session ID. There are edge cases but for typical short chats it works.
[06:00] Miguel: I'm going to show a quick curl example as well as the Node SDK snippet. (shares code) curl -X POST /v1/chat -d '{"model":"redwood-chat-3b","messages":[...]}' -H 'Authorization: Bearer ...' - stream: true
[06:45] Miguel: See here — you can also pass stream: false to wait for final. Streaming gives better perceived latency but you pay for all generated tokens as usual.
[07:10] Ben: How does pricing break down? Per-token? and embeddings separate?
[07:20] Samantha: Hosted is per-token generation and per-embedding when used. We have detailed tier examples in the pricing sheet I'll send. Dedicated committed capacity flips to monthly reserved GPU pricing with slot-based throughput.
[07:45] Miguel: One thing to highlight: for cost/latency tuning use max_tokens and stop sequences, and consider using a smaller model like 3b for many queries; fallback routing can automatically route to cheaper variants under load if you enable it.
[08:10] Priya: For our 20 qps baseline and 80 qps bursts, would you recommend hosted or dedicated?
[08:20] Miguel: Typically hosted is fine for that scale; if you need strict latency SLAs or isolation, Dedicated is better. We'll run a quick estimate and share. (note: we agreed Miguel will compute in follow-up)
[08:50] Samantha: Quick demo of the Console traces — here's a per-request latency breakdown, token cost, and model used. You can filter by route, user token, and time window.
[09:20] Miguel: Also showing Optimize recommendations — it suggests batching window tweaks and optionally quantization on selected models to cut cost. For chat, batching needs to balance latency vs throughput.
[09:55] Priya: Do you support automatic batching in the hosted API or is that a Dedicated feature?
[10:05] Miguel: We do smart batching in hosted but Dedicated gives more control over batch sizes and GPU pooling. Hosted uses workload-aware batching under the hood.
[10:30] Liam: Any limits on concurrent streams per token?
[10:35] Miguel: Default per-account concurrency limits exist; they can be raised with Dedicated or enterprise plans. We can show your account limits in the console.
[11:00] Speaker 1: question about model rollout and version pinning — how do we avoid regressions?
[11:07] Samantha: Our rollouts let you pin a model version per-route, do canary traffic split, and do evals against a prompt set. Optimize can watch quality regressions and alert.
[11:35] Miguel: we'll also show a short example of retry semantics for 429s and 5xxs. We use exponential backoff with jitter and implement safe idempotency for the chat messages.
[12:00] Miguel: Now a short live stream — sending a prompt for summarization. (typing) Streaming tokens: "In Q3 fintech saw a consolidation of payments providers..." Partial tokens arrive every ~40ms.
[13:10] Priya: Looks good, latency is solid. How do you measure tokenization differences across models?
[13:20] Miguel: We include tokenization in the cost estimator; different models/architectures can tokenize differently so the console shows token counts pre/post.
[13:50] Marta: For compliance we need audit logs and user-level RBAC — do you keep per-token logs?
[13:58] Samantha: We keep per-request audit logs and can retain at the level you need, plus SSO/SAML and RBAC are supported for enterprise. We'll include the audit log format in the pack.
[14:30] Miguel: On reliability, we do multi-region fallback and model-variant fallback. If a region is degraded, traffic can failover to another region with minimal interruption.
[15:00] Priya: Curious about the KV cache — can we disable it for some routes?
[15:05] Miguel: Yes, caching policies can be set per-route or per-model; some customers disable cache for sensitive PII content.
[15:30] Ben: Any gotchas with streaming and retries? We've seen duplicate segments when resuming in other vendors.
[15:40] Miguel: Good call — duplicates can happen; our SDK de-duplicates tokens using token IDs and session offsets when resuming, but clients should also be idempotent-aware. We'll share the SDK resume docs.
[16:10] Samantha: Quick talk on onboarding — free credits, quickstart templates, and sample dashboards. We'll also do a POC with a small reserved testing window if you want benchmarks.
[16:35] Priya: We do want to run a small POC, measure cost & latency on our prompts.
[16:45] Samantha: Great, we'll set up POC scoping next week. Miguel will run a hosted vs dedicated cost estimate and we'll send the benchmark template.
[17:05] Miguel: One last note on edge cases: streaming with function calling — if you need structured tool outputs, we can stream partial JSON blobs and the SDK helps reconstruct them.
[17:30] Marta: ok security follow-up: can you confirm encryption in transit + at rest and BYOK options?
[17:38] Samantha: Yes to both — we use TLS in transit and AES-256 at rest, and we support BYOK for Dedicated/Private. See security pack.
[18:05] (small cross-talk, background noise)
[18:30] Samantha: Recap of next steps: send pricing + security pack, schedule POC scoping for 12/08, Miguel to run latency/cost estimate, Priya to provide prompts and traffic profile.
[18:50] Priya: Sounds good. Thanks both.
[19:00] Meeting end.

Notes: transcript likely has occasional mis-transcriptions (e.g., K V cache spelled out). Links mentioned: SOC2/security pack (link: https://redwood.example/security/soc2), pricing sheet (link: https://redwood.example/pricing), benchmark template (link: https://redwood.example/benchmarks/orion).
